extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and practitioners of experimental/computational mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and methodological standards for computational discovery, high-precision numerics, recognition of constants, integer-relation searches, and the conjecture→proof workflow in experimental mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient-precision iterations
rubrics_metrics.description: When using iterative algorithms (e.g., Borwein-type AGM iterations for π), each iteration can dramatically increase correct digits but only if all iterations are performed to at least the precision required for the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the quoted quartic convergence to 1/π 'each iteration approximately quadruples the number of correct digits, provided all iterations are performed to at least the precision required for the result.' Ensure working precision is increased appropriately at each step to avoid loss of digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical checking before formal inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify conjectured/formulaic identities numerically before committing them to exposition or publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borwein wished to computationally check Ramanujan-type formulas (e.g., R1(1,1)) before recording them in a book; initial attempts may give misleading results if convergence is slow or precision inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to convergence issues and numerical pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical experiments must consider convergence behavior; some parameter values can yield much slower convergence and hinder discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: convergence of a continued fraction was slowest in the simplest case (a = b), which hindered early numerical identification of log 2. Test convergence, try alternative representations, and avoid blind reliance on raw numeric outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce dimensionality for efficient numerical integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform multi-dimensional integrals into lower-dimensional (preferably one-dimensional) integrals when possible to enable high-precision numerical evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cn integrals were converted to one-dimensional integrals involving the modified Bessel function K0(t), enabling high-precision evaluation using quadrature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized high-precision quadrature algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: For accurate numeric integration at very high precision, employ robust quadrature schemes designed for high-precision work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example used in the paper: the tanh-sinh quadrature algorithm was used to compute Ising-class integrals to high precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use high-precision computation and integer-relation algorithms (PSLQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute numeric constants to very high precision and apply integer-relation detection (PSLQ and variants) to discover algebraic or linear relations among constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors used high-precision computations (sometimes needing supercomputers) together with Ferguson’s PSLQ to find experimental evaluations of integrals (e.g., D3, D4, En values). High precision and appropriate PSLQ parameters are crucial for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust PSLQ parameters (degree, precision) experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuning PSLQ inputs such as the trial polynomial degree and working precision is necessary to find minimal polynomials or integer relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: they generated the vector (1, α, α^2, ..., α^d) and experimented on the degree d; success depended on choosing d and precision appropriately. Use multipair PSLQ variants for larger problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize representations for numerical speed and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Find alternative analytic formulas that compute the same quantity more rapidly and stably for numerical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: φ2(x,y) was computed much more rapidly by expressing it via theta functions (θ1..θ4) with q = e^{−π} and z = π/2 (y + i x), and using the Fourier-series expressions for the theta functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symbolic-recognition tools to identify constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools like the Inverse Symbolic Calculator (ISC) or database searches to recognize numeric constants arising from computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after computing R(2) numerically, dividing by 2 and querying ISC suggested the value π/2 − log(1 + √2), guiding a conjecture that could be proved. Maintain and consult online resources (OEIS, ISC) when numeric constants appear unfamiliar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallel computing and optimized software for extremely large computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large high-precision computations (tens of thousands of digits or large-degree polynomials) may require parallel implementations and optimized high-precision packages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their later computations were >150× faster using improved packages, multipair PSLQ, and parallel computers; they required up to 64,000-digit precision, degrees up to 512 and huge integer coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolically verify numeric discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: After discovering a candidate relation or polynomial numerically, perform symbolic verification to confirm it is exact (e.g., check minimal polynomial property in a CAS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after PSLQ returned integer-coefficient polynomials, they used Mathematica to ensure the polynomial was in fact the minimal polynomial satisfied by α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computational discovery as a path to rigorous proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat numerical discovery as a tool for forming conjectures which then should be proved analytically or symbolically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative repeatedly shows the pattern: compute high-precision values → recognize patterns/identify constants → form conjectures → seek and obtain proofs (e.g., Kimberley’s formula, limits of Cn). Experimental results motivate and guide rigorous mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check and research computed phenomena in literature/databases
rubrics_metrics.description: After observing surprising numerical patterns, search the literature and databases (e.g., OEIS, published papers) for connections or prior results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Google searches and OEIS (A218147) helped connect computed polynomial sequences to earlier work (Savin and Quarfoot) and guided subsequent proofs and verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for computational expense and selective testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every case can be exhaustively tested due to cost; computational experiments often test many cases up to feasible bounds and leave some instances untested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They confirmed Kimberley’s formula for s up to 52 (except a handful too expensive), and for s=60 and 64. Report limits of computational verification and be transparent about untested exceptions.
